references.text: "Guard your heart above all else you guard, for life flows from it." Luke 8:15 speaks of a "good and noble heart" that receives the Word – this connects to Proverbs' emphasis on the importance of the heart.
Jeremiah writes that the Lord examines the heart and tests the kidneys. The good heart in Luke 8:15 stands in contrast to the deceitful heart, showing how God looks for a sincere heart.

Ezekiel prophesies that God will give a new heart and a new spirit. The "good and noble heart" that receives God's word in Luke 8:15 can be seen as the fulfillment of this promise of a transformed heart.
Matthew's parallel to the parable of the sower: those who hear the word and understand it bear fruit – some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold. This is the direct parallel to Luke 8:15.
Mark's parallel to the parable of the sower: those who hear the word, receive it, and bear fruit, thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. The same message as in Luke 8:15.

Paul writes that God will give eternal life to those who with perseverance in good deeds seek glory, honor, and immortality. The connection to "perseverance" (ὑπομονή) is directly parallel to Luke 8:15.
The fruit of the Spirit – love, joy, peace, patience, etc. – describes the fruit that the good heart bears according to Luke 8:15.

Paul prays that the Colossians may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, bearing fruit in every good work and being strengthened with all power for all perseverance and patience. Both fruit-bearing and perseverance are linked together, as in Luke 8:15.
"For you need perseverance so that you may do God's will and receive what is promised." Perseverance (ὑπομονή) is the central concept that is also key in Luke 8:15.
James urges us to receive with meekness the word planted in you, which has power to save your souls. This mirrors Luke 8:15 where those who hear the word hold fast to it in a good heart.
James writes that the testing of faith produces perseverance, and that perseverance must lead to a complete work. Perseverance as a prerequisite for fruit-bearing is parallel to Luke 8:15.

Peter encourages adding to faith virtue, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly kindness, and love – so that one may not be unfruitful. Fruit-bearing through perseverance connects to Luke 8:15.
